title: TCS and Rolls-Royce Run Jet Engine on 100% Hydrogen Through Full Flight Cycle
excerpt: In an industry first, a modified Rolls-Royce Pearl 15 engine completed take-off, cruise, and landing on pure hydrogen at NASA's Stennis Space Center, capping a four-year propulsion program.
body:
• Rolls-Royce and TCS ran a modified Pearl 15 aero gas turbine through a complete simulated flight cycle — take-off, cruise, and landing — using 100% hydrogen, the first time this has been done on this class of engine.
  • TCS joined the program in 2024 as Rolls-Royce's engineering partner, handling fuel system and engine controls integration, hydrogen combustion analysis, and detailed design across the test campaign at NASA's Stennis Space Center.
  • The milestone validates hydrogen combustion propulsion at engine level but significant challenges remain, including cryogenic storage, new aircraft tank designs, and airport refueling infrastructure.

What the Test Proved

Rolls-Royce and Tata Consultancy Services confirmed on August 14, 2026, that they had operated a modern aero gas turbine through a fully simulated flight cycle using 100% hydrogen at NASA's Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. The modified Rolls-Royce Pearl 15 engine reached full take-off power, held cruise thrust, and throttled back for landing — all without burning a drop of conventional jet fuel.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=HAV0BLzVlS4

The test validated three critical hydrogen propulsion technologies simultaneously: combustion, fuel delivery systems, and engine controls. That integration matters because much of the hydrogen propulsion work to date has stayed at the demonstrator stage, proving hydrogen can burn cleanly in isolation but not that a full engine control system can manage it through the throttle swings of a real flight profile.

"Through a rigorous and carefully staged testing approach, we have gained valuable insights into how 100% hydrogen behaves in a modern aero gas turbine across a full flight cycle while validating critical combustion, fuel and control system technologies."

— Adam Newman, Chief Engineer, Hydrogen Demonstrator Programme, Rolls-Royce

Four Years in the Making

The hydrogen demonstrator program began in 2022 as a partnership between Rolls-Royce and easyJet, the British budget airline that supported the project as part of its long-term decarbonization ambitions. TCS joined in 2024, contributing engineering expertise across fuel system and engine controls integration, hydrogen combustion analysis, test preparation, validation, data analytics, risk management, and detailed design.

The program followed a deliberately incremental path. Early engine testing took place at Boscombe Down in the UK, followed by component and system rig tests across UK and European facilities, including a full-scale hydrogen test facility at the UK Health and Safety Executive. The technology was then integrated into the modified Pearl 15 demonstrator engine for the NASA Stennis campaign.

NASA, the UK Health and Safety Executive, and easyJet all contributed alongside Rolls-Royce and TCS, giving the test both an airline's operational perspective and regulatory input from early in the process.

The Bigger Picture for Aviation

Aviation accounts for roughly 2 to 3% of global CO2 emissions, a share expected to grow as passenger traffic increases across Asia, the Middle East, and emerging markets. Sustainable aviation fuel reduces emissions but does not eliminate them at the point of combustion. Hydrogen burned directly in a modified gas turbine has the potential to eliminate in-flight CO2 emissions entirely.

Rolls-Royce is pursuing hydrogen combustion — burning hydrogen directly inside a turbine to produce thrust. This differs from the fuel-cell approach taken by Airbus in its ZEROe program, which converts hydrogen into electricity to drive electric motors. Both paths aim to decarbonize flight, but combustion sits closer to how jet engines already work, requiring adaptation rather than architectural reinvention.

Newman said the findings would support future propulsion innovations, including Rolls-Royce's UltraFan next-generation engine architecture.

India's Role in Global Aerospace R&D

TCS's role as engineering partner on a flagship aerospace propulsion program reflects the expanding capabilities of Indian IT services firms in deep engineering domains. The work goes well beyond traditional software outsourcing into core aerospace R&D — fuel system design, combustion analysis, and engine controls integration.

Anupam Singhal, President of Manufacturing at TCS, framed the milestone as proof that the industry can move past concept-stage work. "This achievement marks a significant step forward, demonstrating not just the viability of hydrogen, but the industry's readiness to translate ambition into execution," he said.

What's Next

A full flight-cycle test on hydrogen is an engine-level milestone, not a certification. Liquid hydrogen must be stored at around minus 253 degrees Celsius, requiring entirely new aircraft tank designs, fuel systems, and airport refueling infrastructure that does not exist at meaningful scale today. Rolls-Royce and TCS have said they will continue their engineering collaboration to advance hydrogen-powered aviation technologies, with findings feeding into the UltraFan program and broader sustainable propulsion development.
